record.paper_title: Padua points and “fake” nodes for polynomial approximation: old, new and open problems
record.original_question: For two-dimensional polynomial approximation, can the approach using mock-Chebyshev points plus regression serve as a viable alternative to the fake-node approach, where original interpolation nodes are mapped to fake nodes and interpolation is performed on the mapped nodes without resampling the original data values?

evidence.quote: Recently two dimensional mock-Chebyshev points plus regression have been investigated [44]. Is this approach an alternative to the “fake” one?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a compact domain (for concreteness, take $\Omega = [-1,1]^2$), and let $f \colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a continuous (or sufficiently smooth) target function. Consider polynomial approximation of $f$ from samples taken on a uniform tensor-product grid $X_n = \{(x_i, y_j) : 0 \le i, j \le n\} \subset \Omega$, where direct polynomial interpolation on $X_n$ is unstable due to the Runge phenomenon.

Two strategies are compared.

(A) Two-dimensional mock-Chebyshev regression. Inside $X_n$, select the subset $M_n \subset X_n$ of "mock-Chebyshev" points: those grid points closest (in a fixed metric) to the nodes of a bivariate Chebyshev-like grid (e.g. tensor-product Chebyshev–Lobatto nodes or Padua points) of cardinality $\dim \mathcal{P}_d^2$, where $\mathcal{P}_d^2$ denotes bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $d$ with $d = d(n) \asymp \sqrt{n}$. Determine the polynomial $p^\ast \in \mathcal{P}_D^2$ (for some $D \ge d$) that interpolates $f$ on $M_n$ and simultaneously minimizes the residual sum of squares on $X_n \setminus M_n$, i.e. solves a constrained least-squares problem.

(B) Fake-node interpolation. Choose a target set $Y_n$ of "fake" interpolation nodes (e.g. Padua or Chebyshev points) in $\Omega$ of the same cardinality as a chosen interpolation subset of $X_n$, and a bijection (mapping basis) $S \colon \Omega \to \Omega$ sending the original sampling locations to $Y_n$. Construct the polynomial interpolant $q^\ast$ on the fake nodes $Y_n$ using the original sample values $f|_{X_n}$ (without resampling $f$), and define the approximant as $q^\ast \circ S$.

Problem. Establish whether strategy (A) (two-dimensional mock-Chebyshev points plus regression) constitutes a viable alternative to strategy (B) (the fake-nodes approach) for bivariate polynomial approximation from samples on a uniform grid. Specifically, provide convergence rates, Lebesgue-constant-type stability estimates, and error bounds for (A) that are comparable to those known for (B), and identify classes of target functions $f$ and configurations $(n,d,D)$ for which one approach is provably superior to the other.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of whether two-dimensional mock-Chebyshev plus regression can replace the fake-nodes approach is explicitly posed as an open question. Recent work has developed bivariate constrained mock-Chebyshev least squares interpolation (e.g. tensor-product and mock-Padua variants) and the multivariate fake-nodes approach independently, but a direct comparison establishing equivalence or superiority of either method does not appear to have been carried out in the literature retrieved.

status_evidence.title: Multivariate approximation at fake nodes - ScienceDirect
status_evidence.snippet: An effective method for interpolating via mapped bases in the multivariate setting has been proposed, referred to as the Fake Nodes Approach (FNA).
status_evidence.claim: The fake-nodes approach in the multivariate (including 2D) setting has been developed but is treated as a distinct methodology from mock-Chebyshev regression.

status_evidence.title: Polynomial approximation of derivatives by the constrained mock-Chebyshev least squares operator
status_evidence.snippet: Constrained mock-Chebyshev least squares interpolation... extended to the bivariate case via tensor product and mock-Padua nodes.
status_evidence.claim: Bivariate mock-Chebyshev regression has been investigated but is not compared head-to-head with the fake-nodes approach.
